claim: The BFF proxies API calls so the SPA makes same-origin requests (CORS disappears), and CSRF is defended by SameSite cookies plus a required custom header.
quote: SameSite means that the cookies are sandboxed to the same site aka DNS registrar name (e.g. *.mycompany.com) ... Ajax calls to have both credentials (the cookie) and a custom header

claim: The BFF authenticates the frontend with a cookie, obtains the access token and forwards it to the remote API — so the remote API keeps its bearer-token auth scheme; the frontend must send a custom anti-forgery header.
quote: authenticates the frontend using its authentication cookie, gets the appropriate access token, and forwards the request to the Remote API with the token attached ... Remote APIs mapped in the BFF always require an additional custom header on API endpoints.

claim: The token handler / BFF pattern requires minimal changes to existing APIs because they keep receiving bearer tokens; the SPA's security code is simplified.
quote: requires minimal changes to existing web apps or microservices ... by outsourcing the OAuth work, the SPA security code is considerably simplified

claim: BFF-local (embedded) endpoints are cookie-authenticated with an anti-forgery header and suit only single-consumer scenarios — logic placed there is not reachable by other clients.
quote: Self-contained variants suit only single-consumer scenarios ... custom header (like x-csrf: 1) that triggers CORS preflight checks

claim: Migrating an SPA to a BFF deletes token storage, refresh/silent-renew and the OIDC JS dependency; the CSRF interceptor is simpler than the previous bearer-token interceptor; login becomes a plain link to /bff/login.
quote: simpler than the previous implementation because we don't have to worry to expose access tokens to 3rd parties ... we ship less code to our users

claim: The BFF exposes management endpoints under /bff for login, logout and querying the current user.
quote: adds endpoints for performing typical session-management operations such as triggering login and logout and getting information about the currently logged-on user

claim: The common BFF failure modes are silent: UseBff() after UseAuthorization() disables anti-forgery with no error, a YARP metadata typo silently drops the token, BFF API endpoints return 401 instead of a redirect, and CORS errors mean the frontend is not same-origin with the BFF.
quote: If UseBff() is placed after UseAuthorization(), anti-forgery enforcement is silently disabled with no error ... A typo in a YARP metadata key fails silently — no token is attached and no anti-forgery check is enforced.

claim: Without server-side sessions the access and refresh tokens live in the protected session cookie; server-side sessions require a store (an EF implementation is provided) and keep the cookie small.
quote: If you do not use server-side sessions, then the access and refresh token will be stored in the protected session cookie ... The default implementation stores the session in-memory, which is useful for testing, but for production you typically want a more robust storage mechanism.

claim: Large claim sets push the ASP.NET Core auth cookie past the browser's 4KB limit; chunking masks it until it causes failures.
quote: Large numbers of claims (e.g., from many roles or large identity tokens) can cause the cookie to exceed the 4KB browser limit

claim: Multi-instance cookie auth requires a shared Data Protection key ring (Redis, Azure Blob, Key Vault or SQL) so cookies encrypted by one instance can be read by another.
quote: keys shared across several instances of a web app so apps can share authentication cookies or CSRF protection across multiple servers

claim: Deploying an ASP.NET Core cookie-based app across multiple instances requires pointing every instance at a shared key store with the same application name.
quote: each instance generating its own keys, meaning when a user logs in with a cookie encrypted by one instance and their next request lands on another instance, the cookie can't be decrypted

claim: Microsoft's BFF guidance lists the costs — operational overhead per extra service, an extra network hop, and probable code duplication — and says the pattern is unsuitable when only one interface interacts with the backend.
quote: Code duplication is a probable outcome of this pattern ... This pattern might not be suitable when: Interfaces make the same or similar requests to the backend. Only one interface interacts with the backend.

claim: Community opinion (2024-25 Reddit/HN threads, summarised) splits on the API-shaping BFF: valuable at multi-client scale, overkill for a single-client startup.
quote: We ended up with four different backends — the maintenance is painful ... If you're a startup, skip it. If you're at scale, it's worth it.

claim: SignalR WebSocket and SSE transports fail through the Duende BFF forwarder because the WebSocket handshake cannot carry the required X-CSRF header; it falls back to long-polling.
quote: the BFF is marking my websockets call as invalid because there's no X-CSRF header present

claim: Native SignalR hub support through the BFF was an open feature request rather than a shipped capability.
quote: SignalR Support for BFF

claim: ASP.NET Core can register cookie and JWT bearer handlers side by side and require any one of multiple schemes, so one API can serve both browser and bearer clients.
quote: you can use the AuthenticationSchemes property to require any one of multiple valid schemes. The authentication middleware will try each listed scheme in order and succeed if any of them validates successfully.

claim: Vite's dev server can proxy path prefixes such as /api and /bff to a backend, which is how a relative-path SPA runs against a BFF locally.
quote: Expects an object of { key: options } pairs. Any requests whose request path starts with that key will be proxied to the specified target.

claim: Duende BFF is free for companies under $1M annual revenue and requires a paid licence above that threshold.
quote: If you as an individual or your company makes less than one million USD revenue per year, you can use Duende BFF absolutely free of cost.

claim: Duende BFF v4 hosts multiple frontends in a single BFF host, removing the one-BFF-per-SPA operational sprawl.
quote: BFF V4.0 introduces the capability to support multiple BFF Frontends in a single host. This helps to simplify your application landscape by consolidating multiple physical BFF Hosts into a single deployable unit.

claim: One-way-door decisions are costly to reverse and warrant deliberation; two-way-door decisions should be made fast and iterated on.
quote: Two-way door decisions are reversible and less impactful. They provide opportunities to experiment, learn, and iterate.

claim: HTML elements like and cannot send an Authorization header, so a bearer-token SPA needs fetch+blob workarounds for protected images and downloads — workarounds a cookie-based BFF makes unnecessary.
quote: An tag cannot send a custom header ... You'll have to make the HTTP call to get the image yourself so you can send that header, for example using the Fetch API.

claim: The access token is meant to be opaque to the client; decoding it in frontend code to read claims is discouraged.
quote: The access token is meant to be opaque to the client application and should be used only as an authentication key ... this is discouraged.

claim: In Keycloak a SPA is configured with Client authentication OFF (public client) while a server-side web app has Client authentication ON (confidential client) — the BFF switch is a toggle plus new redirect URIs.
quote: for web applications, Client authentication should be ON, Standard flow should be ON, and for single-page applications, Client authentication should be OFF with Standard flow ON

claim: Wiring a React SPA to a Duende BFF is a small amount of code: a claims hook calling /bff/user with an X-CSRF header, login/logout links, and API routes forwarded via MapRemoteBffApiEndpoint.
quote: Create a claims hook that calls /bff/user with an X-CSRF header ... a working example in under 100 lines of React code

claim: Third-party cookie deprecation is complete across major browsers, so a cookie-based BFF must be deployed same-site with the SPA.
quote: every major browser has completed its third-party cookie deprecation, with Chrome removing third-party cookies for all users
